question.problem: The maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+16{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ when ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4,$ is $20.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?
question.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 16 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $20,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=20.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-20I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{aligned}]-20[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-16 & 16 \\ 16 & -16\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-20I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get  

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
